docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of this block diagram is to show the electrical architecture of my individual subsystem for the Handheld LiDAR Accessibility Aid. My subsystem is the Data Collection Board, which is responsible for receiving scan and trigger information, coordinating scan data, and sending collected information to the Interpretation Board.

The diagram shows the microcontroller, communication interfaces, power connections, and connections to the other team members' subsystems.

The main parts of my subsystem include:

  • Microcontroller: PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano
  • Power: VLOGIC and GND supplied by the team Power Board
  • Data collection: Receives LiDAR/scanning and trigger information
  • Communication: UART interfaces are used for communication between boards
  • Team connections: J1 connects to the Trigger Board, J2 connects to the Laser/Scanning Board, and J3 connects to the Interpretation Board
  • Data processing: The microcontroller coordinates scan information, scan position, and buffered samples

The Data Collection Board receives power from the team Power Board rather than generating its own primary power. The power and signal connections are separated so that the diagram clearly shows the difference between power distribution and communication signals.

docs.title: Individual Block Diagram
docs.text: Figure 1: Individual block diagram for Khun Oo's Data Collection Board.

docs.title: Microcontroller
docs.text:
The main microcontroller for my subsystem is the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The microcontroller is responsible for coordinating the incoming scan and trigger information and communicating the collected data with the other subsystems.

The microcontroller includes the following communication interfaces:

  • UART1: Communication with the Trigger Board through J1
  • UART3: Communication with the Laser/Scanning Board through J2
  • UART5/PPS: Communication with the Interpretation Board through J3
  • Data processing: Coordinates scan data, scan position, and buffered samples

The specific MCU I/O pins and signal connections are shown directly in the block diagram.

docs.title: Team Connections
docs.text:
My Data Collection Board connects to three other team subsystems:

Connector Connected Board Purpose Interface J1 Trigger Board Trigger and scan request communication UART J2 Laser/Scanning Board LiDAR/scanning data communication UART J3 Interpretation Board Sends collected data for interpretation UART

The team uses 8-pin ribbon cable connectors. Only the signal pins are counted as microcontroller I/O pins; power and ground are not counted as signal pins.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The Data Collection Board receives power from the team Power Board.

The primary power connection shown on the block diagram is:

  • VLOGIC
  • GND

The final nominal voltage, regulation information, and maximum available current will be updated when the team finalizes the power architecture.

docs.title: Communication Signals
docs.text:
The communication connections use digital serial UART signals. Each UART connection uses two signal lines:

  • TX — transmit
  • RX — receive

The signal connections are bidirectional where required because data can be transmitted and received between the connected boards.

The team ribbon-cable convention is:

  • Pin 1: Collection TX / Remote RX
  • Pin 2: Collection RX / Remote TX
  • Pin 8: GND
  • Remaining pins: reserved or not currently assigned

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Data Collection Board is responsible for coordinating LiDAR scan data, scan position information, and trigger information before sending the collected data to the Interpretation Board.

The current design uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the main microcontroller. The board communicates with the Trigger Board, Laser / Scanning Board, and Interpretation Board through UART connections.

The Data Collection Board receives power from the team Power Board through the P1 power connection. Power and communication are kept separate in the team architecture.

docs.text:
Connector Connected Board Interface Purpose J1 Trigger Board UART TX/RX Receives scan requests and trigger information J2 Laser / Scanning Board UART TX/RX Exchanges LiDAR and scanning information J3 Interpretation Board UART TX/RX Sends collected information for interpretation

The Laser / Scanning Board documentation specifies 3.3 V UART signals for the J2 connection to the Data Collection Board. Therefore, 3.3 V logic is currently used as a design assumption for the Data Collection Board.

Note: The microcontroller was selected for the project and therefore does not require a three-option component-selection comparison. It is still included in the power budget because it consumes power.

docs.title: Power Architecture
docs.text:
The Data Collection Board does not contain its own battery or primary system power source. Power is supplied by the team's Power Board.

The Power Board contains the battery pack, protection and switching circuitry, voltage regulation, and power distribution circuitry.

The Data Collection Board receives power through:

  • P1 — VLOGIC
  • P1 — GND

The UART ribbon cables J1, J2, and J3 are used for communication and are separate from the primary power connection.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
The current design keeps the Data Collection Board focused on data coordination. Its primary purpose is to receive, organize, buffer, and transmit information between the other embedded-system boards.

The LiDAR, scan motor, audio system, vibration motor, battery, and main voltage regulators belong to other team subsystems and therefore are not included as loads in the Data Collection Board power budget.

The current architecture will be updated as the PCB schematic, component selections, and final team power specifications are developed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This Bill of Materials (BOM) identifies the components required to construct the Data Collection Board for the ASU RAS 304 Embedded Systems project.

The board is designed around the KNO PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller. Its power system accepts a +9V input and regulates it to +5V using an LM7805 linear voltage regulator. Additional components support circuit protection, debugging, and external communication interfaces.

All component selections are based on the supplied KiCad schematic. DigiKey is the selected vendor for component sourcing.

The BOM includes planning quantities for breadboard prototyping, final PCB assembly, and spare components.

docs.title: Component Selection and Verification
docs.text:
The following considerations apply before finalizing the hardware order:

  • U2 – Microcontroller: The Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is the primary controller. Confirm whether this development board is already supplied by ASU before purchasing.
  • U1 – Voltage Regulator: The STMicroelectronics L7805CV is a candidate for the LM7805 circuit. Verify its package, pin configuration, and PCB footprint.
  • F1 – Fuse: The schematic identifies a fuse but does not specify its current rating, voltage rating, or physical package. Final selection requires verification.
  • C1 – Capacitor: A 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor is retained as specified in the schematic. The 0805 package is a proposed footprint.
  • R1 and R2 – Resistors: The original resistance values of 330 Ω and 10 kΩ are retained. The 0805 package is proposed for PCB assembly.
  • D1 – Debug LED: The selected red LED is a candidate. Verify its color, dimensions, polarity, and PCB footprint.
  • SW1 – Debug Button: The B3FS-1000P is a candidate for the specified Omron B3FS switch. Verify the exact footprint before ordering.

docs.title: External Interfaces
docs.text:
The schematic also provides three external communication interfaces:

Interface Connections Purpose Trigger RX, TX, GND Trigger communication Laser / Scanning RX, TX, GND Laser and scanning communication Interpretation RX, TX, GND External interpretation interface

These interfaces are represented by signal connections in the current schematic. Physical connectors, mating cables, and mounting hardware must be selected once their footprints and connection requirements are finalized.

docs.title: Important verification notes
docs.text:
• No schematic materials or values have been changed. The DigiKey selections are candidate purchasable parts where the schematic does not specify a full manufacturer part number.
  • F1: The schematic only says Fuse. It does not give current rating, voltage rating, time-delay/fast-blow characteristic, size, or holder. This line cannot be responsibly completed or ordered yet.
  • D1: The schematic only says DEBUG LED. Color and package are unspecified. The red 5 mm part is only a candidate.
  • SW1: The schematic identifies the Omron B3FS family. Verify the exact B3FS suffix and PCB footprint before purchase.
  • U1: The schematic uses a custom LM7805_KNO symbol and has no footprint. The L7805CV is a 5 V 7805-family TO-220 candidate; verify pin order and footprint.
  • C1, R1, R2: Footprints are blank. 0805 packages are proposed as a minimum-size planning choice; verify against your PCB.
  • U2: Confirm whether the Curiosity Nano board is already supplied by the course/team before ordering.

* Quantities are planning estimates. For discrete components, 3 = one prototype/breadboard part, one final PCB part, and one spare. For U2, 2 = one board plus one spare. Confirm quantities and availability at checkout.

Not included as BOM components: Trigger, Laser/Scanning, and Interpretation are net labels/interfaces in the supplied schematic, not separate connector symbols with defined part numbers or footprints. Add physical connectors only after selecting their actual footprints and mating cable requirements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is designed to support a data collection board utilizing a KNO_PIC18F57043_Curiosity_Nano microcontroller. It features a +9V power input regulated down to +5V via an LM7805 linear regulator, protected by a fuse (F1). External communication and sensing interfaces include Trigger (RX, TX, GND) and Laser/Scanning (RX, TX, GND) ports connected to the microcontroller's UART/digital lines, alongside an Interpretation breakout interface, a DEBUG LED, and a DEBUG Button (SW1).

Figure 1: Example schematic of the Data Collection Board.
